title: Peter weeps bitterly (Matthew 26:57–75)
hookLine: a trial inside, a servant girl outside, and Peter's own voice gives him away
tomorrow: Judas brings the silver back. what do they say to him?

lines: OUTSIDE: THOU ALSO WAST WITH HIM.
cards: Split screen, like a series cutting between two rooms. Inside the house of Caiaphas the high priest, Jesus is on trial. Outside in the courtyard, Peter, who followed afar off, sits with the servants to see how it ends.
Two rooms, two men, and in both of them the same question: who are you, really? Inside, false witnesses come and go. "But Jesus held his peace."
Under oath he answers once: "Thou hast said." Outside, a servant girl looks at Peter: "Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee."

teach.h: I DO NOT KNOW THE MAN.
teach.b: Peter: "I know not what thou sayest." Another maid says the same, and he swears: "I do not know the man."
Then the bystanders: "Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee." His way of talking gives him away. He curses and swears again.

"And immediately the cock crew. And Peter remembered the word of Jesus... And he went out, and wept bitterly." So what are tears like his for? Christians answer in two ways, and both have a real case.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: STAY IN THE SORROW.
teach.b: One view: sorrow like Peter's is holy, worth staying in. Its case: a failure taken lightly will happen again, and the psalm says, "a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."
Peter doesn't explain himself or blame the girl. He goes out and weeps, and some Christians see that as the honest beginning of turning around.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: LOOK UP TO GRACE.
teach.b: The other view: don't stay in the tears; the turning point is grace, not how hard you cry. Its case: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins."
Sorrow that never looks up for forgiveness can turn into despair, and the person stays stuck. Both views agree on one thing in this scene: Matthew doesn't hide Peter's worst night.
He tells it in full, and he ends the chapter on his tears.

how: Some churches read Peter's denial in Holy Week, and in some Christian art Peter is shown beside a rooster, a reminder of this night; some Christians bring failures like his to confession or to prayer.

games.q: peter weeps bitterly — tap the pairs.

s: Peter denied Jesus to armed soldiers who threatened him
a servant girl, another maid, and the bystanders. the danger in Matthew is a question.
Jesus answered every charge at his trial
"But Jesus held his peace." he speaks under oath, once.
when the cock crew, Peter remembered what Jesus had said
"Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly."

games.q: your friend blew it badly. she says: crying about it is pointless, just move on. you agree with her. what's the best case for the other side?
o: honest sorrow takes the failure seriously; God won't despise a broken heart.
feeling awful for long enough pays off what you did.
tears prove you were a good person all along.
games.why: the sorrow view rests on Psalm 51:17 and on Peter, who doesn't explain himself but goes out and weeps. the grace view rests on 1 John 1:9. Christians hold both.

practice: On a piece of paper, write one failure in a single plain line, the kind of thing you'd rather nobody knew. Read it once, slowly, without explaining it away.
Then fold the paper and hold it in a closed hand while you breathe, letting it be as heavy as it is, no heavier and no lighter.
